shinyOAuthDB

shinyOAuthDB helps you build Shiny apps that query a database or data platform using each app user’s own account. People sign in with the account they already use for that data source, and your app queries data on their behalf.

This is useful when you or your organization already manage accounts and data permissions in a database or data platform. Your Shiny app can reuse those permissions, so you don’t have to maintain a separate set of user accounts and data-access rules in the Shiny app. For example, if your database limits an analyst to sales data for their region, your Shiny dashboard can query the data as that analyst and automatically use the same restriction.

The OAuth sign-in and data access work like this:

  1. A user navigates to your Shiny app. Your Shiny app shows a Sign in button (shinyOAuth can also redirect users to the provider automatically). When the user clicks this button, the app uses shinyOAuth to start the OAuth sign-in flow. The user is sent to the sign-in page of the database or data platform, or to a trusted sign-in service (like your organization’s login service).
  2. The user signs in with their existing account and, if asked, approves the access your app requests.
  3. They return to your Shiny app and shinyOAuth obtains an access token, a temporary credential that lets your Shiny app request data on their behalf.
  4. Your Shiny app uses shinyOAuthDB to send that token with its data requests. The database or data platform checks the token and applies that user’s permissions before returning data.

shinyOAuthDB provides R functions to streamline the above steps, with configurations for various databases and data platforms. It also helps you open database connections, run queries, and make API calls. Depending on the data source, you can work with familiar tools such as DBI and dbplyr, or use a supporting package’s query and API helpers.

Supported databases and data platforms (links open their setup guides):

PostgreSQL · PostgREST · DuckDB (over Quack) · Trino and Starburst · Databricks · Microsoft Fabric and Power BI · Snowflake · Google BigQuery · Amazon Redshift · Amazon Athena · Azure SQL and SQL Server · Azure PostgreSQL · Azure MySQL · Google Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL · Azure Cosmos DB for NoSQL · Supabase · Oracle Database · Oracle REST Data Services · MongoDB · Elasticsearch · OpenSearch · Neo4j · SAP HANA and HANA Cloud · Salesforce CRM and Data Cloud · ClickHouse · SingleStore · StarRocks · libSQL and Turso · CockroachDB · Dremio · CrateDB.

Install

The example below installs missing packages from CRAN. To install the development version from GitHub instead:

if (!requireNamespace("remotes", quietly = TRUE)) {
    install.packages("remotes")
}
remotes::install_github("lukakoning/shinyOAuthDB")

Example usage with PostgreSQL

Below is a minimal example of a Shiny app that queries a PostgreSQL database.

It launches PostgreSQL and Keycloak sign-in in Docker (so install and launch Docker if you wish to run it).

This example uses PostgREST since it does not require a database driver to be installed, but you could also use DBI with a PostgreSQL driver. See the PostgreSQL guide for that.

library(shiny)
library(shinyOAuth)
library(shinyOAuthDB)

# Launch a local demo with PostgreSQL and Keycloak sign-in in Docker
demo <- oauth_db_demo("postgrest", action = "services")

# Set up the OAuth client for the demo provider
client <- oauth_client(
  demo$provider,
  client_id = "shiny-db",
  client_secret = "demo-client-secret",
  redirect_uri = "http://localhost:18100",
  scopes = c("openid", "profile", "database.read")
)

ui <- oauth_ui(
  fluidPage(
    actionButton("login", "Sign in"),
    actionButton("logout", "Sign out"),
    actionButton("load", "Load rows"),
    textOutput("account"),
    tableOutput("rows")
  ),
  id = "auth",
  client = client
)

server <- function(input, output, session) {
  # Set up the OAuth module server to handle sign-in and sign-out
  auth <- oauth_module_server(
    "auth",
    client,
    auto_redirect = FALSE,
    async = TRUE
  )

  # Login and logout buttons trigger the OAuth flow and sign-out, respectively
  observeEvent(input$login, auth$request_login())
  observeEvent(input$logout, auth$logout())

  # Show whether the user is signed in
  output$account <- renderText({
    if (is.null(auth$connection())) "Not signed in" else "Signed in. Click Load rows."
  })

  # Retrieve data from the database using the user's access token
  postgres <- oauth_db_postgrest_api(auth$connection, url = demo$url)  
  query_task <- oauth_db_task(postgres, method = "select")

  # Button to load rows from the database; the query runs in the background
  observeEvent(input$load, {
    query_task$invoke("visible_rows", order = "row_id.asc")
  })

  # Display the query results in a table
  output$rows <- renderTable(query_task$result())
}

runApp(
  shinyApp(ui, server, uiPattern = ".*", onStart = function() {
    mirai::daemons(2)
    onStop(function() {
      mirai::daemons(0)
      demo$stop()
    }
  }),
  port = 18100,
  launch.browser = FALSE
)

# Open the app in your regular browser at http://localhost:18100
# (viewers in RStudio/Positron/etc. cannot perform necessary redirects)

Sign in as alice / alice or bob / bob (username / password). The first build takes a few minutes; your browser may ask you to accept the local sign-in certificate. Stopping the app removes its Docker services.

For your own PostgreSQL server, follow the PostgreSQL or PostgREST guides. For other databases and data platforms, refer to the links above.

Learn more

Getting started walks through this app, explains OAuth settings, and covers connections, sessions and saved results. Use the source guides above for the setup and query methods specific to your database or data platform.

More demos

The package includes various demo apps.

oauth_db_demo() runs local Docker demos for PostgreSQL and other self-hosted databases. oauth_db_cloud_demo() guides demos for several cloud platforms, during which you will be walked through first setup with your existing platform workspace and account.

See Getting started, ?oauth_db_demo and ?oauth_db_cloud_demo for the demo options.
